source.title: Revisiting Intermediate Layer Distillation for Compressing Language Models: An Overfitting Perspective
source.authors: Jongwoo Ko; Seungjoon Park; Minchan Jeong; S. Hong; Euijai Ahn; Duhyeuk Chang; Se-Young Yun

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares distillation methods and reports held-out GLUE performance under standard, few-sample, and label-noise conditions, addressing overfitting and generalization through a different training intervention. It does not test the listed claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports comparisons of intermediate-layer distillation (ILD), prediction-layer knowledge distillation (KD), and its proposed consistency-regularized ILD (CR-ILD). Its Gaussian-embedding-noise results are described in figures without numeric values and measure training loss, not the magnitude-aware sharpness in V7.
record.test_reason: The study investigates generalization in language-model distillation, but none of its results tests V1–V8. Partial label corruption does not test fitting fixed random labels; embedding perturbations and loss-surface visualizations do not measure V7's magnitude-aware weight sharpness or its ranking of generalization gaps. Reporting batch-size choices and using dropout do not test their effects.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that intermediate-layer distillation can overfit target-task data, that last-layer distillation and suitable supplementary tasks can alleviate this, and that their MixUp-based consistency regularization improves standard and ill-conditioned GLUE performance. They also report consistent benefits in supplementary T5 experiments.
record.recipe_differences: Studies language-model distillation with BERT/T5 students and teachers, including intermediate-layer objectives, supplementary-task training, and MixUp-based consistency regularization; it does not use the original claim's random-label memorization experiments or listed interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with layer mapping, target versus supplementary task, dataset size, effective sequence length, task similarity, student initialization, and label-noise rate. The paper reports that last-layer ILD's advantage narrows with larger datasets and well-pretrained students.

fits_no_version.finding: For Truncated BERT, standard-GLUE averages are 78.9 for KD, 76.0 for TinyBERT, and 80.1 for CR-ILD. Corresponding averages are 67.8, 64.2, and 69.7 with 1,000 training examples, and 74.1, 71.4, and 75.3 with 30% label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Consistency-regularized intermediate-layer distillation improves held-out GLUE performance over these KD and TinyBERT baselines in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 4 and 8 report training-loss robustness to Gaussian noise injected into embeddings; Appendix E.1 visualizes loss in a plane defined by differences between trained parameter vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distillation strategies differ in embedding-noise robustness and visualized loss geometry; these measures are distinct from magnitude-aware weight sharpness.

record.problems: The reported averages are held-out development performance, not explicit train-test gaps. The supplied table text is flattened, so some Table 1 method-to-average assignments cannot be recovered. Some robustness analyses are presented only in figures without numeric values. The authors limit their experiments mainly to sentence classification and note that token classification and question answering remain future work.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-task values and ablations in Tables 1–6 and Figures 1–12 are not extracted here; the row limit was not reached, but those results concern particular distillation methods rather than any listed claim version. Gaussian-embedding-noise training-loss curves are figure-only and do not report numeric values.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels, natural-label generalization with the same recipe, and chance-level held-out accuracy for random labels.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Large versus small batches under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that alter the penalty.
The effect of adding, varying, or removing dropout on held-out error.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with measured generalization gaps at similarly low training loss, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equal-sized random removals and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain unlinked to the listed versions; cannot_determine denotes their inability to establish those effects, not uncertainty about the readable Table 2 values. The Table 1 Truncated BERT averages are recoverable from the supplied text. These method-performance rows belong under fits_no_version and warrant no version-level verdict.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fit or held-out performance comparison is reported.
No network-width sweep past the interpolation threshold is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-network comparison is reported.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison is reported.
The paper studies MixUp-based consistency regularization and distillation, not dropout.
Embedding-noise tolerance and loss-surface results do not measure magnitude-aware weight perturbation tolerance or rank generalization gaps against the tested norm and margin measures.
The paper does not remove memorized training examples and retrain.
